# Example 16: $\Diamond \Box A \rightarrow \Box \Diamond A$ in S4

## Example 16: $\Diamond \Box A \rightarrow \Box \Diamond A$ in S4

---

\begin{oltableau}
[\sFmla{\False}{1, \Diamond \Box A \rightarrow \Box \Diamond A}, checked, just = \TAss
    [\sFmla{\True}{1, \Diamond \Box A}, checked, just = {\TRule{\False}{\rightarrow}[1]}
        [\sFmla{\False}{1, \Box \Diamond A}, just = {\TRule{\False}{\rightarrow}[1]}
            [\sFmla{\True}{1.1, \Box A}, just = {\TRule{\True}{\Diamond}[2]}
            ]
        ]
    ]
]
\end{oltableau}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
![$\Diamond \Box A \rightarrow \Box \Diamond A$](../images/tableaux-11/tableau-11-58.tex.svg){width=600px}
:::

Assume the formula is false at world 1. True $\Diamond$ (line 2) introduces world 1.1, where $\Box A$ holds. False $\Box$ will introduce a second world once we apply it to line 3 — but first let's continue developing world 1.1.

---

\begin{oltableau}
[\sFmla{\False}{1, \Diamond \Box A \rightarrow \Box \Diamond A}, checked, just = \TAss
    [\sFmla{\True}{1, \Diamond \Box A}, checked, just = {\TRule{\False}{\rightarrow}[1]}
        [\sFmla{\False}{1, \Box \Diamond A}, checked, just = {\TRule{\False}{\rightarrow}[1]}
            [\sFmla{\True}{1.1, \Box A}, just = {\TRule{\True}{\Diamond}[2]}
                [\sFmla{\False}{1.2, \Diamond A}, just = {\TRule{\False}{\Box}[3]}
                ]
            ]
        ]
    ]
]
\end{oltableau}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
![$\Diamond \Box A \rightarrow \Box \Diamond A$](../images/tableaux-11/tableau-11-59.tex.svg){width=600px}
:::

False $\Box$ (line 3) introduces world 1.2, where $\Diamond A$ is false. We now have two accessible worlds from 1: world 1.1, where $\Box A$ holds, and world 1.2, where $\Diamond A$ is false.

---

\begin{oltableau}
[\sFmla{\False}{1, \Diamond \Box A \rightarrow \Box \Diamond A}, checked, just = \TAss
    [\sFmla{\True}{1, \Diamond \Box A}, checked, just = {\TRule{\False}{\rightarrow}[1]}
        [\sFmla{\False}{1, \Box \Diamond A}, checked, just = {\TRule{\False}{\rightarrow}[1]}
            [\sFmla{\True}{1.1, \Box A}, just = {\TRule{\True}{\Diamond}[2]}
                [\sFmla{\False}{1.2, \Diamond A}, just = {\TRule{\False}{\Box}[3]}
                    [\sFmla{\True}{1.1, A}, just = {\TRule{\Box}{\text{T}}[4]}
                        [\sFmla{\False}{1.2, A}, just = {\TRule{\Diamond}{\text{T}}[5]}
                        ]
                    ]
                ]
            ]
        ]
    ]
]
\end{oltableau}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
![$\Diamond \Box A \rightarrow \Box \Diamond A$](../images/tableaux-11/tableau-11-60.tex.svg){width=600px}
:::

The T$\Box$ rule gives $A$ true at 1.1 (line 6), and the T$\Diamond$ rule gives $A$ false at 1.2 (line 7). There is no contradiction: lines 6 and 7 are about **different worlds**, and in S4 there is no rule that connects them. The tree stays open.

## Countermodel for S4

The open branch describes a model:

::: {.incremental}
- Three worlds: $w_1$, $w_{1.1}$, $w_{1.2}$. World $w_1$ accesses both $w_{1.1}$ and $w_{1.2}$; each world accesses itself (T condition). Worlds $w_{1.1}$ and $w_{1.2}$ do **not** access each other.
- $A$ is **true** at $w_{1.1}$ and **false** at $w_{1.2}$.
- Since $w_{1.1}$ only accesses itself and $A$ is true there, $\Box A$ is true at $w_{1.1}$ — so $\Diamond \Box A$ is true at $w_1$.
- Since $w_{1.2}$ only accesses itself and $A$ is false there, $\Diamond A$ is false at $w_{1.2}$ — so $\Box \Diamond A$ is false at $w_1$.
:::

. . .

This is an S4 frame (reflexive and transitive): the only chains of length 2 run through self-loops, so transitivity holds vacuously. But $w_{1.1}$ and $w_{1.2}$ are "side by side" — neither can see the other — and that is exactly what S4 cannot rule out.

# Example 17: $\Diamond \Box A \rightarrow \Box \Diamond A$ in S5

## Example 17: $\Diamond \Box A \rightarrow \Box \Diamond A$ in S5

In **S5** we have the additional **5 rule** (euclidean condition): if two worlds are both accessible from the same world, they can access each other.

So since worlds 1.1 and 1.2 are both accessible from world 1, the 5 rule tells us that 1.1 can access 1.2. Let's pick up where we left off.

---

\begin{oltableau}
[\sFmla{\False}{1, \Diamond \Box A \rightarrow \Box \Diamond A}, checked, just = \TAss
    [\sFmla{\True}{1, \Diamond \Box A}, checked, just = {\TRule{\False}{\rightarrow}[1]}
        [\sFmla{\False}{1, \Box \Diamond A}, checked, just = {\TRule{\False}{\rightarrow}[1]}
            [\sFmla{\True}{1.1, \Box A}, just = {\TRule{\True}{\Diamond}[2]}
                [\sFmla{\False}{1.2, \Diamond A}, just = {\TRule{\False}{\Box}[3]}
                    [\sFmla{\True}{1.1, A}, just = {\TRule{\Box}{\text{T}}[4]}
                        [\sFmla{\False}{1.2, A}, checked, just = {\TRule{\Diamond}{\text{T}}[5]}
                            [\sFmla{\True}{1.2, A}, just = {\TRule{\True}{\Box}[4]}, close]
                        ]
                    ]
                ]
            ]
        ]
    ]
]
\end{oltableau}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
![$\Diamond \Box A \rightarrow \Box \Diamond A$](../images/tableaux-11/tableau-11-61.tex.svg){width=600px}
:::

The T$\Diamond$ rule gives $A$ false at 1.2 (line 7, with line 5 now checked). But True $\Box$ (line 4) is reusable: since the 5 rule gives us that 1.1 accesses 1.2, it fires at world 1.2, giving $A$ true there. This contradicts line 7. The branch closes. This formula is **valid** in **S5**.

## Why is this valid?

::: {.incremental}
- Assume $\Diamond \Box A$ at $w_1$: some accessible world $w_{1.1}$ has $\Box A$.
- Assume for contradiction that $\Box \Diamond A$ fails at $w_1$: some accessible world $w_{1.2}$ has $\Diamond A$ false, meaning $A$ is false at every world accessible from $w_{1.2}$.
- By the T condition, $w_{1.2}$ accesses itself, so $A$ is false at $w_{1.2}$.
- By the 5 rule (euclidean condition), since $w_1$ accesses both $w_{1.1}$ and $w_{1.2}$, world $w_{1.1}$ accesses $w_{1.2}$.
- But $\Box A$ is true at $w_{1.1}$, so $A$ must be true at every world accessible from $w_{1.1}$ — including $w_{1.2}$. Contradiction.
:::

. . .

The euclidean condition is essential: it "connects" the two accessible worlds $w_{1.1}$ and $w_{1.2}$, allowing $\Box A$ at $w_{1.1}$ to reach $w_{1.2}$ and override the false $\Diamond A$ there. Without it, those worlds remain isolated from each other.
